source.title: An asymptotic formula for integer points on Markoff-Hurwitz varieties
source.authors: Alex Gamburd, Michael Magee and Ryan Ronan
readSections: Historical extraction record, Claude Code cc-fb70e5, 2026-09-22: the entire arXiv v3 (57 pages, §§1–5 and references) was read; published text was not obtained then. Historical independent review cc-442dc5 on 2026-09-23 likewise read arXiv v3.

Fresh fix collation, Codex codex-J6LwjP, 2026-09-30: read the complete publisher PDF, Annals 190 (2019), pp.751–809, including references. Compared selected preprint passages and inspected the published Jacobian table and bounds as page images. The publisher PDF is publicly available; the earlier access failure is historical. summary: Gamburd–Magee–Ronan prove a positive leading-term asymptotic c(log R)^β for unexceptional integer points on Markoff–Hurwitz varieties, using descent, accelerated polynomial moves, linear-semigroup comparison and transfer-operator renewal theory. The published Annals text has been read in full and collated with arXiv v3 at all recorded findings. The inventory has 50 items: 1 library, 1 planned and 48 missing, routed once across CA.4 and three coalesced Part II proposals. PM.4 supplies only the base Gauss dynamics; its conjugacy and C¹ spectral theory are missing. The scalar Tauberian theorem shares Wood’s existing owner, while its uniform renewal application belongs to the transfer design. E7 and E11 are corrected in print; E2, E4, E5, E8 and E17 are partly corrected; E18 is the surviving Jacobian typo. The 17 historical preprint reviews remain in versionHistory. The new published collation and E18 await independent review. Published Examples 16–17 are included, with the latter’s deferred proof recorded. No formalization or completion of the open blueprint proofs is claimed.

items.name: The Markoff–Hurwitz equation, its tuples and moves
items.statement: For integers n ≥ 3, a ≥ 1 and k, V = V_{n,a,k} ⊂ 𝔸ⁿ is x₁² + … + x_n² = a x₁x₂⋯x_n + k (1.1); its integer points are Markoff–Hurwitz tuples, counted in the ℓ^∞ ball B(R). The move m_j replaces x_j by the other root a∏_{i≠j}x_i − x_j of (1.1) viewed as a quadratic in x_j. For n = 3, a = 3, k = 0 the positive solutions are the Markoff triples.
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source. The n=a=3,k=0 positive-integer specialization is already planned in CA.4: positive-markoff-triples, markoff-vieta-involution, markoff-descent-inequality and markoff-root-generation. Import those nodes; the general (n,a,k) carrier, exceptional families and compact-set descent remain missing on source route 1. The n=3,a=1 level-k specialization coalesces with PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/3,4,7,8; do not define a second carrier.

items.name: Exceptional solutions (Definition 15, Remark 4)
items.statement: x ∈ V(ℤ₊) is fundamental exceptional if, after ordering, either a = 1, x₁ = … = x_{n−3} = 1, x_{n−2} = 2 (then x ∈ V iff (x_{n−1} − x_n)² = k − n − 1), or a = 2, x₁ = … = x_{n−2} = 1 (then x ∈ V iff (x_{n−1} − x_n)² = k − n + 2). E is the Aut(V)-orbit of these. E ≠ ∅ only if a ∈ {1, 2} and k − n − 1, resp. k − n + 2, is a square, and then |E ∩ B(R)| ≥ cR for R ≥ R₀; being exceptional is Aut(V)-invariant.
items.locator: Definition 15, Remark 4, pp.3, 11–12, arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Definition 15, pp.765–766; Remark 4, p.754.
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Passage from V(ℤ) to V(ℤ₊) (§2.1)
items.statement: |(V(ℤ) − E) ∩ B(R)| = 2^{n−1}|(V(ℤ₊) − E) ∩ B(R)| + O_{n,k}(1): points with a zero coordinate are finite in number, the even sign-change group N acts freely on the rest, and orbits containing no all-positive representative are O_{n,k}(1) in number, since x̃₁² + … + x̃_n² + a x̃₁⋯x̃_n = k has finitely many positive solutions.
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 16 (behaviour of the moves outside a compact set)
items.statement: There is an ℓ^∞ ball K₀ = K₀(n, a, k), which may be enlarged, such that for unexceptional x ∈ V(ℤ₊) − K₀: (1) the move at the largest coordinate strictly decreases the maximum; (2) the largest entry is unique; (3) a move at a non-largest coordinate makes it the largest; (4) such a move does not decrease the number of distinct entries; (5) every move maps V(ℤ₊) − K₀ into V(ℤ₊).
items.locator: Proposition 16 and proof, pp.13–15, adapting Cassels [Cas57, p.27], arXiv:1603.06267v3 (error E3 in the scope of part 3); Annals (2019): Proposition 18, pp.767–770.
items.note: Statement as corrected in E3: part (3) holds outside K₀, not for all x ∈ V(ℤ₊). Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Corollary 17 (infinite descent)
items.statement: Every unexceptional Markoff–Hurwitz tuple can be reduced algorithmically to one in K₀ by moves that strictly decrease the maximal entry. For n = a = 3, k = 0 every Markoff triple reduces to (1, 1, 1) (Markoff); for n = a > 3, k = 0 (Hurwitz) and more generally for k = 0, there are finitely many fundamental solutions, characterised by Baragar when a ≥ 2(n − 1)^{1/2}.
items.locator: Corollary 17, p.15, citing [Mar80], [Hur07], [Bar94b], arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Corollary 19, p.770.

items.name: Automorphisms of the Markoff–Hurwitz variety
items.statement: Aut(V), the polynomial automorphisms of V(ℂ), is G ⋊ (N ⋊ S_n), where N is the group of even sign changes (|N| = 2^{n−1}), S_n permutes coordinates, and G is generated by the moves m_j (Horowitz [Hor75] for n = 3, Hu–Tan–Zhang [HPZ15, Theorem 1.1] for n ≥ 4). In particular V(ℤ) is Aut(V)-invariant.
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22). Review: the paper calls Aut(V) the polynomial automorphisms of V(ℂ), but the cited results (Horowitz; Hu–Tan–Zhang, Theorem 1.1) concern polynomial automorphisms of ℂⁿ preserving the polynomial Σx_i² − a∏x_i, not of a single fibre. Only the explicit group G ⋊ (N ⋊ S_n) is used, so read Aut(V) as that group.

items.name: Theorem 1 (McShane–Rivin)
items.statement: The number M(R) of Markoff triples (x, y, z) with x ≤ y ≤ z ≤ R is C(log R)² + O(log R log log R) with C > 0.
items.locator: Theorem 1, p.2, citing [MR95] (after Gurwood, Zagier [Zag82], Belyi), arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Theorem 1, p.753.
items.note: Cited, the n = 3 endpoint; equivalently a count of simple closed geodesics on the modular torus. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Theorem 2 (Baragar) and the exponent β(n)
items.statement: There is β = β(n) such that for k = 0, if V(ℤ) − {0} ≠ ∅, then for every ε > 0, Ω((log R)^{β−ε}) ≤ |V(ℤ) ∩ B(R)| ≤ O((log R)^{β+ε}); in fact |V(ℤ) ∩ B(R)| = (log R)^{β+o(1)} [Bar98], with β(3) = 2, β(4) ∈ (2.430, 2.477), β(5) ∈ (2.730, 2.798), β(6) ∈ (2.963, 3.048) and log(n − 1)/log 2 < β(n) < log(n − 1)/log 2 + o(n^{−0.58}).
items.note: Cited. Used in §4.3 to identify the pole β₀ of the resolvent with Baragar's β. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Theorem 3 (asymptotic formula for Markoff–Hurwitz tuples)
items.statement: For each (n, a, k) with V(ℤ) − E infinite there is c = c(n, a, k) > 0 such that |(V(ℤ) − E) ∩ B(R)| = c(log R)^β + o((log R)^β), with β = β(n) as in Theorem 2.
items.locator: Theorem 3, p.3; proof §3.1, pp.21–22, given Proposition 21, arXiv:1603.06267v3 (misprints E2; positivity gap E1); Annals (2019): Theorem 3, p.754; proof using Proposition 23, pp.776–777.
items.note: The exponent depends only on n. Sanity check made in this extraction: counting the orbit of (1,1,1,1) for n = a = 4, k = 0 up to R = 10^640 gives local slopes d log N/d log log R ≈ 2.44, inside Baragar's interval. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Normalisation and the polynomial semigroup Λ
items.statement: z = a^{1/(n−2)}x satisfies z₁² + … + z_n² = z₁⋯z_n + k′ with k′ = ka^{2/(n−2)} (2.4). M is the set of ordered such tuples in a^{1/(n−2)}ℤ₊ⁿ, K = a^{1/(n−2)}K₀ (2.5), and λ_j(z) = (z₁, …, ẑ_j, …, z_n, ∏_{i≠j}z_i − z_j) for 1 ≤ j ≤ n − 1 (2.6), which preserve M − K. Λ = Λ(n) is the semigroup of piecewise polynomial maps generated by the λ_j, and α(z) = ∏_{j≤n−2}z_j.
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Lemma 18 (freeness of Λ)
items.statement: If z₀ ∈ M − K has distinct entries then λ ↦ λ(z₀) is injective on Λ; hence Λ is free on {λ_j} (as a semigroup of polynomial maps), using the infinite orbit of (1, …, 1) for a = n, k = 0.
items.locator: Lemma 18 and proof, pp.16–17, arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Lemma 20, pp.771–772.
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Lemmas 19–20 (admissible sequences, multiplicities, reduction to (2.8))
items.statement: For x ∈ V(ℤ₊) − K₀, the map φ_x from finite admissible move sequences (no move at the current largest coordinate) to V(ℤ₊) is injective, and images of φ_x, φ_{x′} are disjoint unless one base lies in the other's image (Lemma 19). For unexceptional x there is a bijection Θ_x : Σ*(x) → Λ intertwining φ_x with z(x′) = order(a^{1/(n−2)}x′) (Lemma 20). Hence V(ℤ₊) − E − K₀ is a finite disjoint union of orbits φ_{x⁽⁰⁾}(Σ*(x⁽⁰⁾)), and Theorem 3 reduces to the asymptotics of Σ_{λ ∈ Λ} 1{(λ.z⁽⁰⁾)_n ≤ R} (2.8) for finitely many unexceptional base points z⁽⁰⁾.
items.locator: §2.3, Lemmas 19–20, (2.8), pp.17–18, arXiv:1603.06267v3 (misprints E4) (missing hypothesis and misprints E13); Annals (2019): Lemmas 21–22, (2.9), pp.772–773.
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Acceleration, the counts M₀ and M, and the renewal equation
items.statement: S_Λ = {λ_{n−1}^Aλ_j : A ≥ 0, 1 ≤ j ≤ n − 2} freely generates Λ′ = ∪_{j ≤ n−2} Λ.λ_j; Λ.z⁽⁰⁾ = ∪_{A₀ ≥ 0} Λ′.λ_{n−1}^{A₀}z⁽⁰⁾ (3.2). M₀(z, a) = Σ_{λ ∈ Λ∪{e}} 1{log log(λ.z)_n − log log z_n ≤ a} (3.3), and M(z, a) is the same sum over Λ′ ∪ {e} (3.4). The shift s deletes the leftmost S_Λ-letter, τ⋆(λ) = log log(λ.z⁽⁰⁾)_n − log log(s(λ).z⁽⁰⁾)_n, τ⋆^N is its N-fold cocycle (3.6), and M(λz⁽⁰⁾, a) = Σ_{λ′ ∈ S_Λ} M(λ′λz⁽⁰⁾, a − τ⋆(λ′λ)) + 1{0 ≤ a} (3.7), iterated L times in (3.8).
items.note: The acceleration imitates Zorich's acceleration of Rauzy–Veech induction. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Lemma 22 (growth along λ_{n−1})
items.statement: For unexceptional z ∈ M − K, (λ_{n−1}^Az)_n ≥ 2^Az_n; more precisely λ_{n−1} acts on the last two entries by [[0, 1], [−1, α(z)]] with α(z) = a x₁⋯x_{n−2} ∈ ℤ₊, α = 1 is impossible, α = 2 forces z exceptional, and for α ≥ 3 the Z_A = (λ^A_{n−1}z)_n satisfy Z_{A+1} = αZ_A − Z_{A−1} ≥ 2Z_A. Likewise (λ^A_{n−1}z)_n ≥ (α(z) − 1)^Az_n.
items.locator: Lemma 22 and proof, p.21 (α(z) is defined on p.20); proof of Lemma 23, p.24, arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Lemma 24, pp.776–777; use in Lemma 25, pp.779–780.
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Proposition 21 (asymptotics of the accelerated count)
items.statement: For every unexceptional z ∈ M − K there is c⋆(z) > 0 with M(z, a) = e^{βa}(c⋆(z) + o(1)) as a → ∞, the rate of decay independent of z and the c⋆(z) uniformly bounded in terms of n. Consequently M₀(z⁽⁰⁾, a) ∼ (log z_n⁽⁰⁾)^β c_∞(z⁽⁰⁾)e^{βa}, which gives Theorem 3.
items.locator: Proposition 21, p.21; proof §§3.2–3.5, pp.22–33, arXiv:1603.06267v3 (gap E1: positivity of c⋆ is not argued); Annals (2019): Proposition 23, p.776; proof pp.778–790.
items.note: Statement with the positivity supplied as in E1. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Lemma 23 (counting words of bounded distortion)
items.statement: There are c₀, c₁ depending only on n with Σ_{λ′ : s^L(λ′) = λ} 1{τ⋆^L(λ′) ≤ x} ≤ c₁^L(c₀ + x)^Le^x for all L ∈ ℕ, x ≥ 0 (3.9), with c₁ = 2(n − 2)(n − 1), using τ⋆(λ^A_{n−1}λ_jλ̃) ≥ log(1 + A/(2(n − 1))) (3.12). For δ > 0 and L = ⌈ca/log a⌉ with c = c(δ), the intermediate sums in (3.8) are O(e^{(1+δ)a}) (3.10) and c₁^L(c₀ + x)^L ≤ e^{δx} for x ≥ a/2 (3.11).
items.locator: Lemma 23 and proof, pp.23–25, arXiv:1603.06267v3 (misprint E5); Annals (2019): Lemma 25, pp.779–781.
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Lemma 24 (doubly exponential growth)
items.statement: There is C > 0 with α(λ′z⁽⁰⁾) ≥ ½exp(Cφ^L) (3.15) and (λ′z⁽⁰⁾)_n ≥ exp(Cφ^L) (3.16) whenever s^L(λ′) = λ, where φ = (1 + √5)/2; the proof uses the two-step recursion Z_p ≥ (Z_{p−1} − 1)Z_{p−2}.
items.locator: Lemma 24 and proof, pp.25–26, arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Lemma 26, pp.781–782.
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Lemma 25 (fitting log z to the hyperplane H)
items.statement: With f(z) = (log z₁, …, log z_{n−1}, Σ_{j≤n−1}log z_j), there are C₁, C₂ depending only on n such that for z ∈ M − K with α(z) > C₁, log z ≤ f(z) ≤ log z + C₂α(z)^{−2}(0, …, 0, 1) (3.20), using z_n = (A(z)/2)(1 + √(1 − 4(C(z) − k′)/A(z)²)).
items.locator: Lemma 25 and proof, p.27, after [Zag82, Lemma 2], arXiv:1603.06267v3 (misprint E6); Annals (2019): Lemma 27, p.783.
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Lemmas 26–27 (the fit is preserved by the moves)
items.statement: For ε > 0, z ∈ M − K with α(z) > max(C₁, 2C₂^{1/2}ε^{−1/2}) and y⁽¹⁾, y⁽²⁾ ∈ H: y⁽¹⁾ + ε(0, …, 0, ½, ½, 1) < f(z) ≤ y⁽²⁾ implies γ_jy⁽¹⁾ + ε(0, …, 0, ½, ½, 1) < f(λ_jz) ≤ γ_jy⁽²⁾ for 1 ≤ j ≤ n − 1 (Lemma 26). With ε = 16C₂exp(−2Cφ^{ca/log a}) (3.23) and y(λ′) = f(λ′z⁽⁰⁾), (1 − ε)y(λ′) + ε(0, …, 0, ½, ½, 1) ≤ y(λ′), strictly in the last three coordinates (Lemma 27, as corrected in E12; the printed strict inequality fails when a = 1 and a coordinate z_i = 1 with i ≤ n − 3). In (3.21)–(3.22) the first n − 3 coordinates are likewise non-strict.
items.locator: Lemmas 26–27 and proofs, pp.28–29, after [Zag82, proof of Lemma 3], arXiv:1603.06267v3 (error E7 in the proof of Lemma 27) (E12: strictness); Annals (2019): Lemmas 28–29, pp.783–785.
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Lemma 28 and (3.25) (comparison with the linear count)
items.statement: Matching λ⁽²⁾ = λ^{A_N}_{n−1}λ_{j_N}⋯λ^{A_1}_{n−1}λ_{j_1} ∈ S^{(N)} with γ⁽²⁾ = γ^{A_N}_{n−1}γ_{j_N}⋯γ^{A_1}_{n−1}γ_{j_1} ∈ Γ′ (a bijection, both being free) gives log log(λ⁽²⁾λ′z⁽⁰⁾)_n ≤ log(γ⁽²⁾.y(λ′))_n ≤ log log(λ⁽²⁾λ′z⁽⁰⁾)_n + 2ε (3.25), hence N(y(λ′), a − τ⋆^L(λ′) − 2ε) ≤ M(λ′z⁽⁰⁾, a − τ⋆^L(λ′)) ≤ N(y(λ′), a − τ⋆^L(λ′) + 2ε) (Lemma 28 with 2ε, as its proof gives; the paper prints ε, E11).
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22).

items.name: Lemma 29 and Proposition 30 (assembling the count)
items.statement: M(λz⁽⁰⁾, a) = (1 + o(1))e^{βa}Σ_{λ′ : s^L(λ′) = λ} e^{−βτ⋆^L(λ′)}h(y′) + O(exp(βa^δ + (1 + δ)a)) uniformly in λ (Lemma 29, via Theorem 13). a_L(λz⁽⁰⁾) = Σ_{λ′ : s^L(λ′) = λ} h(y(λ′))e^{−βτ⋆^L(λ′)} converges as L → ∞ to c⋆(λz⁽⁰⁾), uniformly in λ, with |a_{L+1} − a_L| ≪ exp(C₄L^{1+η} − 2Cφ^L) by the recursion (1.8), and the limits are uniformly bounded (Proposition 30).
items.locator: Lemma 29, Proposition 30 and proofs, pp.30–33, arXiv:1603.06267v3 (E10: summation step in the proof of Proposition 30); Annals (2019): Lemma 31, pp.786–788; Proposition 32, pp.788–790.

items.name: Connections to simple closed geodesics (§1.1)
items.statement: Theorem 1 counts simple closed geodesics of length ≤ log R on the modular torus (McShane–Rivin for all hyperbolic once-punctured tori; Mirzakhani for general surfaces). For n = a = 4, k = 0, V(ℝ₊) parametrises the Teichmüller space of RP² minus three points, and the number n_J^{(1)}(L) of one-sided simple closed geodesics of length ≤ L satisfies log n_J^{(1)}(L)/log L → β(4) (Huang–Norbury), with n_J^{(1)}(L) ∼ cL^{β(4)} (Magee [Mag17]). Hu–Tan–Zhang describe regions where Aut(V) acts properly discontinuously and prove a McShane identity.
items.note: Context, not used in the proofs. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22). Review: a Markoff number m corresponds to a geodesic of trace 3m, so of length 2 arccosh(3m/2) = 2 log m + O(1); the rephrasing needs length ≤ 2 log R + O(1), not log R (E14).

items.name: The linear semigroups Γ, Γ′, the hyperplane H and ∆
items.statement: γ_j(y) = (y₁, …, ŷ_j, …, y_n, Σ_{i≠j}y_i) for 1 ≤ j ≤ n − 1 (1.4); Γ = ⟨γ₁, …, γ_{n−1}⟩₊ and Γ′ = ⟨T_Γ⟩₊ with T_Γ = {γ^A_{n−1}γ_j : A ≥ 0, 1 ≤ j ≤ n − 2}, both free. They preserve H = {y ∈ ℝⁿ_{≥0} : y₁ ≤ … ≤ y_n, Σ_{j≤n−1}y_j = y_n} (1.5), which has basis e_j = (0, …, 1_j, …, 0, 1), and ∆ = H/ℝ₊. For n = 3, Γ′ is generated by [[0, 1], [1, A + 1]] (continued fractions, Example 8) and σ(a, b, a + b) = order(b − a, a, b) inverts both γ_j (the Euclidean algorithm, Example 7). For n = 4 the projective action of Γ is, up to permutations, the Rauzy gasket IFS (Example 9), and for n ≥ 4, ∆ ≠ ∪_jγ_j(∆).
items.note: Routed to the new Part II ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartIITransferOperators.

items.name: The linear orbit count N(y, a)
items.statement: N(y, a) = Σ_{γ ∈ Γ′∪{e}} 1{log(γ.y)_n − log y_n ≤ a} for y ∈ H − 0, a ≥ 0 (1.7); it is invariant under y ↦ ty, t > 0, so descends to ∆.
items.note: Routed to the new Part II ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartIITransferOperators.

items.name: Theorem 13 (linear semigroup count)
items.statement: There is a positive bounded C¹ function h on H, invariant under ℝ₊, such that N(y, a) = h(y)e^{βa}(1 + o(1)) as a → ∞ uniformly in y ∈ H − 0; h satisfies Σ_{γ ∈ T_Γ}((γ.y)_n/y_n)^{−β}h(γ.y) = h(y) (1.8). β is Baragar's exponent.
items.locator: Theorem 13, p.9; proof §§4.1–4.5 given Proposition 43, arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Theorem 13, p.759; proof §§4.1–4.5, pp.790–800.

items.name: Theorem 10 and Lemma 42 (β as a conformal exponent)
items.statement: β is the unique s ∈ (1, ∞) for which there is a probability measure ν_s on ∆ with ∫f dν_s = Σ_{γ ∈ T_Γ}∫f(γ.w)|Jac_w(γ)|^{s/(n−1)}dν_s(w) for all f ∈ C⁰(∆) (a conformal measure). This rests on (γ.w)_n/w_n = |Jac_w(γ)|^{−1/(n−1)} for γ ∈ Γ (Lemma 42), so the condition is L*_βν = ν. By analogy with Patterson–Sullivan theory (Remark 11), but β is not evidently a Hausdorff dimension of the limit set; for n = 4, ν_β is essentially the Avila–Hubert–Skripchenko measure on the Rauzy gasket (Remark 12).
items.locator: Theorem 10, Remarks 11–12, p.7; Lemma 42, p.40, arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Theorem 10, Remarks 11–12, p.759; Lemma 44, p.797.

items.name: Remark 14 (monotonicity of β)
items.statement: The (n − 1)-dimensional H embeds in the n-dimensional one compatibly with the semigroups, so Theorem 13 gives β(n) ≥ β(n − 1); in particular β(n) ≥ 2 for all n ≥ 3.

items.name: Renewal equation and transfer operator L_s
items.statement: N(y, a) = Σ_{γ ∈ T_Γ}N(γ.y, a − log(γ.y)_n + log y_n) + 1{0 ≤ a} (4.1). On ∆, with coordinates w = (w₁, …, w_{n−1}, 1), w₁ ≤ … ≤ w_{n−1}, Σw_j = 1, the Laplace transform N̂(w, s) = ∫e^{−sx}N(w, x)dx satisfies N̂ = s^{−1}(1 − L_s)^{−1}1 (4.2), (4.4), where L_s[f](w) = Σ_{γ ∈ T_Γ}(w_n/(γ.w)_n)^s f(γ.w) (4.3). Explicitly γ^A_{n−1}γ_j[w₁, …, w_{n−1}, 1] = [w₁, …, ŵ_j, …, w_{n−1}, 1 + A(1 − w_j), 1 + (A + 1)(1 − w_j)] (4.5), so (γ.w)_n = 1 + (A + 1)(1 − w_j) (4.6) and L_s[f](w) = Σ_{j ≤ n−2}Σ_{A ≥ 0}(1 + (A + 1)(1 − w_j))^{−s}f(γ^A_{n−1}γ_j.w) (4.7).

The generic scalar Tauberian theorem is item 48, owned by the Wood route rather than this transfer-operator Part II.

items.name: The base Gauss map and its invariant probability measure
items.statement: On (0,1], the Gauss map T(x)={1/x}, with T(0)=0 by convention, has inverse branches x↦1/(x+m), m≥1. Its invariant probability measure on [0,1] has Lebesgue density 1/((1+x)log 2). The unnormalized function 1/(1+x) is a fixed function of the usual s=2 Gauss transfer operator; the spectral simplicity/gap and conjugacy with the GMR operator are separate missing items 44–45.

items.name: Real and complex p-series summability
items.statement: For real p, Σ_{n≥1}n^(−p) converges iff p>1. For complex p, Σ_{n≥1}n^(−p) is summable iff Re p>1, with complex powers of positive real integers; equivalently the absolute-value series converges there.

items.name: Lemma 33 and Corollary 34 (L_s on C⁰ and its eigenmeasures)
items.statement: For ℜ(s) > 1 the series (4.3) converges absolutely and uniformly on ∆ (using w_j ≤ 1/2 for j ≤ n − 2), so L_s : C⁰(∆) → C⁰(∆) is bounded. For each real s > 1 there are λ_s > 0 and a probability measure ν_s with L*_sν_s = λ_sν_s (by the Schauder–Tychonoff theorem).

items.name: Schauder–Tychonoff fixed point theorem
items.statement: A continuous self-map of a nonempty compact convex subset of a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space has a fixed point; applied to ν ↦ L*_sν/(L*_sν)(1) on probability measures on ∆ with the weak-* topology.
items.locator: Corollary 34, p.36, arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Corollary 36, p.792.

items.name: Lemma 36 and Lemma 44 (C¹ theory and the Ionescu-Tulcea–Marinescu inequality)
items.statement: For ℜ(s) > 1, s ↦ L_s is a holomorphic family of bounded operators on C¹(∆) (norm ‖f‖_∞ + ‖∇f‖_∞), shown by truncating the A-sum and controlling the tail in C¹. There is C > 0 with ‖∇L_s^Q[f](w)‖₂ ≤ C|s|L_σ^Q[|f|](w) + Dρ^QL_σ^Q[‖∇f‖₂](w), σ = ℜ(s) for all Q ∈ ℕ, ℜ(s) > 1, w ∈ ∆ (Lemma 44, from Proposition 43 and the chain rule).
items.locator: Lemma 36, p.36; Lemma 44 and proof of Lemma 36, pp.41–42, citing [ITM50], arXiv:1603.06267v3 (E15: L_s printed for L_{ℜ(s)}); Annals (2019): Lemma 38, p.793; Lemma 46 and proof of Lemma 38, pp.798–799.
items.note: Routed to the new Part II ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartIITransferOperators. C¹(∆) with the value-plus-derivative sup norm is not a pinned library carrier. Item 46 and the route brief require its construction in the affine span, completeness, inclusion of 1 and bounded composition. ContDiffMapSupportedIn consists of global C¹ functions vanishing outside a compact set and cannot supply this carrier. The countable-sum/two-norm arguments remain explicit obligations.

items.name: Theorem 37 (Ruelle–Perron–Frobenius for L_s)
items.statement: For real s ∈ (1, ∞) and L_s : C¹(∆) → C¹(∆): (1) λ_s is a simple eigenvalue and the rest of the spectrum lies in a disc of radius R(s) < λ_s, with λ_s − R(s) ≥ ε(I) > 0 uniformly for s in each compact I ⊂ (1, ∞); (2) ν_s is the unique probability measure with L*_sν_s = λ_sν_s; (3) the eigenfunction h_s with ν_s(h_s) = 1 is positive.
items.locator: Theorem 37, pp.36–37; proof sketched in §4.4, p.42, via [Liv95] or [Pol, Lemma 2.3], arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Theorem 39, pp.793–794; proof sketch p.799.
items.note: The paper sketches the proof (Birkhoff cones or Pollicott's method with Lemma 44); the design must write it out for countably many branches on C¹(∆). Routed to the new Part II ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartIITransferOperators. Chosen source route: adapt the Liverani [Liv95] cone/Hilbert-projective-metric method, using the paper-specific two-norm estimate, uniform contraction, compact C¹→C⁰ control and summable branch weights. The countably many branches and possibly thin invariant set require a proof; a finite-type PP90 theorem does not apply unchanged. The alternative direct Pollicott citation is bibliographically ambiguous between versions and is retained as an unresolved source identification, not a claimed proof read.

items.name: The limit set K(Γ′)
items.statement: Since the elements of T_Γ uniformly contract ∆ (Proposition 43), (γ⁽¹⁾, γ⁽²⁾, …) ↦ lim_j γ⁽¹⁾⋯γ⁽ʲ⁾.w₀ is well defined and independent of w₀; its image K(Γ′), the attractor of the iterated function system T_Γ, is a compact Γ′-invariant subset of ∆.
items.note: Routed to the new Part II ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartIITransferOperators.

items.name: Definition 38 and Theorem 39 (Wielandt's theorem after Pollicott)
items.statement: f = u + iv on T_Γ × ∆ is regular if no r ∈ ℝ and bounded G : K(Γ′) → ℝ satisfy v(γ, w) − G(γ.w) + G(w) − r ∈ 2πℤ on T_Γ × K(Γ′). If F_s(γ, w) = −s log((γ.w)_n/w_n) is regular, ℑ(s) ≠ 0 and ℜ(s) > 1, then the spectral radius of L_s on C¹(∆) is strictly less than λ_{ℜ(s)}.
items.locator: Definition 38, Theorem 39, pp.37–38, citing Pollicott [Pol84, Theorem 2] and Wielandt [Wie50], arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Definition 40, p.794; Theorem 41, p.795.
items.note: Pollicott proved it for subshifts of finite type; the paper asserts the proof carries over. Routed to the new Part II ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartIITransferOperators.

items.name: Proposition 40 (non-lattice property)
items.statement: For all s ∈ ℂ − ℝ the function (4.8) is regular. Proof: at fixed points of γ^A_{n−1}γ_{n−2} (eigenvector v₊ = (0, …, 0, 1, T₊, T₊(T₊ − A)) ∈ H with T₊ = (A + 1 + √((A + 1)² + 4))/2 from det(γ − T) = (1 − T)^{n−3}(−T)(T² − (A + 1)T − 1)), the cocycle takes the values log T₊(A), whose successive gaps are nonzero and tend to 0, so no translate of a discrete subgroup contains them.
items.locator: Proposition 40 and proof, pp.38–39, arXiv:1603.06267v3; Annals (2019): Proposition 42, pp.795–796.
items.note: Routed to the new Part II ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartIITransferOperators.

items.name: Proposition 41 (the leading eigenvalue)
items.statement: s ↦ λ_s is real analytic and strictly decreasing on (1, ∞), with λ_s → 0 as s → ∞; hence at most one β₀ ∈ (1, ∞) has λ_{β₀} = 1. Proof: λ_s ≤ 2^s(n − 2)Σ_{A ≥ 0}(3 + A)^{−s}, log λ_s = N^{−1}log L_s^N[1](w) + o(1) uniformly, and log((γ.w)_n/w_n) ≥ N log(3/2) for γ ∈ (T_Γ)^N.
items.locator: Proposition 41, p.39; proof §4.5, pp.42–43, arXiv:1603.06267v3 (misprint E8); Annals (2019): Proposition 43, p.796; proof pp.799–800.
items.note: Statement unchanged; E8 corrects the displayed bound. Routed to the new Part II ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartIITransferOperators.

items.name: Analytic perturbation of an isolated simple eigenvalue (Kato)
items.statement: If s ↦ L_s is a holomorphic family of bounded operators and L_{s₀} has an isolated simple eigenvalue λ_{s₀}, then near s₀ there are holomorphic λ_s, h_s, ν_s with L_sh_s = λ_sh_s, L*_sν_s = λ_sν_s, ν_s(h_s) = 1, and a holomorphic complementary part; with P_s = ν_s(·)h_s and L′_s = L_s(1 − P_s), with the additional resolvent hypothesis λ_{s₀}=1 and the rest of the spectrum strictly inside the unit disk, so 1 ∉ spec(L′_s) near s₀ and away from λ_s=1: (1 − L_s)^{−1} = λ_s(1 − λ_s)^{−1}P_s + (1 − L′_s)^{−1}. The paper prints (1 − λ_s)^{−1}ν_s(g)h_s + (1 − L′_s)^{−1}g, which cannot hold at g = h_s; the pole at λ_s = 1 and its residue are the same (E16).
items.note: Imported functional analysis; no atlas layer owns it. Routed to the new Part II ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartIITransferOperators.

items.name: The paper-specific Tauberian application, residue and uniform renewal estimate
items.statement: Let β₀>1 satisfy λ_{β₀}=1. For each w∈∆, N(w,·) is nonnegative, nondecreasing and locally finite, and is zero at negative times. Its complex Laplace transform converges for Re s>β₀ and equals s⁻¹(1−L_s)⁻¹1. The spectral/non-lattice theorems extend it holomorphically near each point of Re s=β₀ except β₀. Normalize ν_{β₀}(1)=ν_{β₀}(h_{β₀})=1. The branch ratio ≥3/2 implies λ′_{β₀}≤−log(3/2)λ_{β₀}<0, and the simple pole has coefficient B(w)=h_{β₀}(w)/(β₀|λ′_{β₀}|)>0. Import the scalar nondecreasing Laplace Tauberian theorem (item 48, PAPER-WOOD-19/286, m=1) to get N(w,a)∼B(w)e^(β₀a) for each fixed w. The uniform-in-w o(1) required by Theorem 13 is a further paper-specific proof obligation: establish uniform analytic/contour estimates in a Banach norm or a uniform Tauberian adapter. Once this uniform estimate is proved, §3 with the positive constant of E1 identifies β₀=β by Baragar. Existence of β₀ follows from λ_s→∞ as s↓1 and λ_s→0 as s→∞, with continuity and the quantitative derivative bound.
items.locator: §4.3, pp.39–40, citing Lalley [Lal88], [Lal89], arXiv:1603.06267v3 (E16: leading constant); Annals (2019): §4.3, pp.796–797.
items.note: Plan only the application hypotheses, residue, existence/identification of β and uniform estimate here. Pointwise asymptotics plus continuity of B do not imply uniform convergence. The waiting time is at least log(3/2), and only finitely many branches occur below a fixed height; convergence right of β follows from the positive operator/branch expansion and spectral radius bound. Generic Tauberian theory has the shared Wood supplier. This remains a source-level proof obligation, not a claimed completed contour proof.

items.name: Proposition 43 (uniform contraction)
items.statement: There are D > 0 and ρ < 1 such that ‖d_w[γ⁽¹⁾γ⁽²⁾⋯γ⁽ᴺ⁾]‖_op ≤ Dρ^N for all γ⁽ⁱ⁾ ∈ T_Γ and w ∈ ∆ (Euclidean metric on ∆); ℓ² may be replaced by ℓ¹ (Remark 45).

items.name: §5: the core/cusp decomposition, bounds (5.1)–(5.10) and Lemma 46
items.statement: In coordinates (w₁, …, w_{n−2}) with β(w) = Σ_{k≤n−2}w_k, let ∆_core = {0 ≤ w_{n−1} − β(w) ≤ w_{n−2}}, ∆_cusp = {w_{n−1} − β(w) ≥ w_{n−2}} and ∆₀ = ∆_core ∪ ∆_cusp; γ_i(∆) ⊂ ∆_core for i ≤ n − 2 and γ_{n−1}(∆) ⊂ ∆_cusp. Explicit ℓ¹ operator norm bounds (maximum absolute column sums) hold: ‖dγ_i‖ ≤ 6/5 on ∆_cusp and 4/3 on ∆_core for i ≤ n − 2 (5.1; the v3 range i ≤ n−3 was corrected to i ≤ n−2 in Annals, E17), with w_{n−2} ≤ ½, w_{n−3} ≤ ¼ on ∆_core and w_{n−2} ≤ ⅓, w_{n−3} ≤ ⅕ on ∆_cusp; ‖dγ_{n−1}‖ ≤ 1 on ∆₀ (5.2); ‖d(γ_i ∘ γ_j)‖ ≤ 4/5 on ∆₀ for i, j ≤ n − 2 (5.3)–(5.5); ‖d(γ_{n−1} ∘ γ_i)‖ ≤ 10/13 on ∆_cusp and 4/5 on ∆_core for i ≤ n − 3 (5.6), and 6/7 and 1 for i = n − 2 (5.7); ‖d(γ_i ∘ γ_{n−1} ∘ γ_{n−2})‖ ≤ 4/7 for i ≤ n − 3 (5.8) and 32/49 for i = n − 2 (5.9); ‖d(γ²_{n−1} ∘ γ_{n−2})‖ ≤ 2/3 on ∆_cusp and 4/5 on ∆_core (5.10). Hence ‖d(γ^L_{n−1} ∘ γ_i ∘ γ^K_{n−1} ∘ γ_j)|_{∆₀}‖₁ ≤ 24/25 for all L, K ∈ ℕ and i, j ≤ n − 2 (Lemma 46); Proposition 43 on all of ∆ follows since one further factor, evaluated possibly outside ∆₀, is bounded and absorbed into D.
items.locator: §§5.1–5.3, (5.1)–(5.10), Lemma 46, pp.43–53, arXiv:1603.06267v3 (misprints E9, E17); Annals (2019): §5, bounds (5.1)–(5.10), pp.801–802; Lemma 48, pp.802–803; Table 1, p.804. Proofs of (5.2)–(5.10) are in the arXiv supplement. New E18 corrects row 3 of the displayed Jacobian; the column-sum bound is unchanged.

items.name: Parameter-dependent Gauss transfer-operator conjugacy
items.statement: For n=3, x∈[0,1] and complex s with Re s>1, let M_s multiply by (x+1)^s, using the real logarithm of positive bases. For T_A(x)=1/(x+A+1), the GMR operator has weight ((x+1)/(x+A+2))^s, and M_s⁻¹ L_s M_s f = Σ_{A≥0}(x+A+1)^(−s) f(T_A(x)). M_s and its inverse are bounded on C¹([0,1]); the sums converge with the regularity required by the transfer theory.
items.locator: arXiv v3 Examples 32,35, pp.35–36; Annals Examples 34,37, pp.791–793
items.note: Import the base map from PM.4; the parameter-dependent weighted conjugacy is missing and routes to the transfer-operator Part II. Check the identity branchwise before exchanging sums.

items.name: The n=3 C¹ spectral theorem and Gauss normalization
items.statement: For real s>1, the Gauss weighted transfer operator on C¹([0,1]) has the n=3 spectral data of GMR Theorem 37 (Annals Theorem 39): a simple positive leading eigenvalue, positive eigenfunction and eigenprobability, and a spectral gap uniform for s in compact subintervals of (1,∞). Via item 44 this supplies the GMR operator. At s=2 the Gauss eigenvalue is 1 with unnormalized eigenfunction 1/(1+x); its invariant probability density is 1/((1+x)log 2). The corresponding GMR eigenfunction is x+1=1/w₂, before any ν(h)=1 rescaling.
items.locator: arXiv v3 Example 35 and Theorem 37, pp.36–37, citing Wirsing [Wir74]; Annals Example 37 and Theorem 39, pp.792–793
items.note: This precise function-space spectral theorem is missing from PM.4, whose scope supplies only the base Gauss dynamics. Plan it once in route 3 as the n=3 specialization of the full RPF theory, with the chosen function space explicit.

items.name: The Banach space C¹(K) on a compact convex body
items.statement: Let K be a nonempty compact convex body with nonempty interior in its finite-dimensional real affine span E. C¹(K;ℂ) consists of functions continuous on K, C¹ on its relative interior, whose derivative extends continuously to K; the extension is unique. Equip it with ‖f‖∞+‖Df‖∞. Supply the complete normed complex vector space, constants, derivative restriction, evaluation, and bounded pullback by C¹ maps K→K with bounded derivative. One construction uses continuous pairs (f,D) satisfying the fundamental-theorem identity along every line segment in K, a closed subspace of C(K;ℂ)×C(K;E→L[ℝ]ℂ).
items.locator: Annals p.793 (C¹ norm), Lemma 38 and its proof pp.798–799; arXiv v3 pp.36,41–42
items.note: Missing infrastructure in route 3, not ContDiffMapSupportedIn. Fix the affine-span convention so boundary derivatives and completeness are meaningful. Mandatory blueprint tests: constant 1 is included with derivative zero; affine functions have their constant derivative; pullbacks compose and satisfy the chain-rule norm bound.

items.name: Complex bilateral Laplace and the renewal/Mellin adapters
items.statement: For suitable complex-valued f on ℝ define Bf(s)=∫ℝ exp(−sx)f(x)dx wherever absolutely integrable. Share the one-sided complex Laplace convention of the Tauberian supplier. Split positive/negative times to obtain Bf(s)=L(f|[0,∞))(s)+L(t↦f(−t))(-s), up to the measure-zero endpoint; for f zero at negative times only the first term remains. Prove convergence and holomorphy on open strips in general and a right half-plane for the renewal count, justify transforming its sum/translation equation, and derive N̂=s⁻¹(1−L_s)⁻¹1. With g(t)=f(log t) for t>0, the change x=log t yields Bf(s)=mellin(g,−s), with the required integrability/change-of-variables hypotheses.
items.locator: arXiv v3 §4.1, p.34, (4.1)–(4.4); Annals pp.790–791; pinned Mathlib/Analysis/MellinTransform.lean:91 supplies only mellin

items.name: Scalar nondecreasing Laplace Tauberian theorem, simple-pole case
items.statement: For β>0 and a nonnegative nondecreasing locally integrable α on [0,∞), suppose F(s)=∫₀∞exp(−st)α(t)dt converges for Re s>β and extends holomorphically near each boundary point except β. If F has a simple pole at β with coefficient B>0, then α(t)∼B exp(βt). This is PAPER-WOOD-19/286 with pole order m=1.

items.name: Published Cayley-cubic Chebyshev polynomial orbit
items.statement: For the Cayley cubic n=3,a=1,k=4, let P_j(t)=2T_j(t/2), with P₀=2, P₁=t and P_{j+1}=tP_j−P_{j−1}, so P_j∈ℤ[t]. Whenever one of h,i,j is the sum of the other two, (P_h,P_i,P_j) lies on the cubic over ℤ[t]. The Vieta moves preserve this family; in particular every coordinate in the orbit of C(t)=(2,t,t) is some P_j.

routes.brief:
Extend Probabilistic, metric and ergodic number theory (ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheory) beyond PM.4's Gauss map. The new layers are transfer operators for uniformly contracting iterated function systems with countably many branches on a simplex, and the renewal method for counting in semigroup orbits. Import from PM.4 the Gauss map, its invariant probability density 1/((1 + x) log 2) and continued fractions. Import the pinned spectralRadius, real/complex p-series summability (including Complex.summable_one_div_nat_cpow), and general bounded-operator/holomorphic-map vocabulary. These imports do not supply Kato spectral perturbation, C¹(K), or a complex Laplace transform. Supply C¹(K) in the affine span with the value-plus-derivative norm, completeness and bounded composition (item 46). Supply the bilateral/zero-extension, Mellin and renewal adapters of item 47, sharing the generic one-sided complex Laplace convention with the Tauberian supplier. Keep Tau Ceti’s real-measure Laplace API as existing work, without treating it as this missing complex transform. Supply in this Part II the Schauder–Tychonoff theorem, Kato's perturbation theory for an isolated simple eigenvalue, and the Ionescu-Tulcea–Marinescu method, unless an owner appears first.

Final theorems, for n ≥ 3 and Γ′ = ⟨T_Γ⟩₊, T_Γ = {γ^A_{n−1}γ_j : A ≥ 0, 1 ≤ j ≤ n − 2}, acting on ∆ = H/ℝ₊:
(1) Uniform contraction: ‖d[γ⁽¹⁾⋯γ⁽ᴺ⁾]‖ ≤ Dρ^N (Proposition 43), via ∆_core, ∆_cusp, the ten explicit ℓ¹ bounds (5.1)–(5.10) and the two-step bound 24/25 (Lemma 46).
(2) For real s > 1, L_s[f](w) = Σ_{j,A}(1 + (A + 1)(1 − w_j))^{−s}f(γ^A_{n−1}γ_j.w) on C¹(∆) has a simple leading eigenvalue λ_s with a uniform spectral gap on compacta, a unique eigenprobability ν_s and a positive eigenfunction h_s (Theorem 37).
(3) For ℑ(s) ≠ 0 the spectral radius is < λ_{ℜ(s)}, by Pollicott's Wielandt theorem and the non-lattice property from the fixed points of γ^A_{n−1}γ_{n−2} (Theorem 39, Proposition 40).
(4) s ↦ λ_s is real analytic and strictly decreasing, → ∞ as s ↓ 1 and → 0 as s → ∞, so there is a unique β with λ_β = 1 (Proposition 41).
(5) Theorem 13: N(y, a) = h(y)e^{βa}(1 + o(1)) uniformly, with Σ_{γ ∈ T_Γ}((γ.y)_n/y_n)^{−β}h(γ.y) = h(y).
(6) Theorem 10: β is the unique s > 1 with a conformal probability measure, using (γ.w)_n/w_n = |Jac_w(γ)|^{−1/(n−1)}.

Principles. Prove existence of β directly (item (4)) rather than through Baragar's theorem. The identification with Baragar's β(n) belongs to the Markoff Part II. Write out the countably-many-branches RPF proof via the Liverani cone method and the paper-specific two-norm inequality; PP90 Theorem 2.2 is a finite-type comparison, not an unchanged supplier theorem. Import the scalar nondecreasing Laplace Tauberian theorem, simple-pole case, from Arithmetic Dirichlet series and Tauberian methods, Part II (accepted alias ArithmeticDirichletSeriesPartIIHigherPoleTauberian, PAPER-WOOD-19/286; canonical DESIGN-ArithmeticDirichletSeriesPartII). Plan here the transform hypotheses, residue B(w)=hβ(w)/(β|λ′β|), and a uniform-in-w analytic/contour or Tauberian adapter. Continuity of B plus pointwise asymptotics is insufficient. Use the branch ratio ≥3/2 to establish λ′β<0, not strict monotonicity alone.

Mandatory examples:
- n = 3: L_s is conjugate to the Gauss transfer operator, and λ₂ = 1 with h = 1/w₂;
- n = 4: the Rauzy gasket;
- a numerical check that λ_s = 1 near s ≈ 2.44 for n = 4;
- the displayed bound λ_s ≤ 2^s(n − 2)Σ(3 + A)^{−s} (not 2(n − 2)Σ…, source issue E8). Review amendments: Lemma 44 holds with L_{ℜ(s)} on the right (E15); the Kato decomposition is (1 − L_s)^{−1} = λ_s(1 − λ_s)^{−1}P_s + (1 − L′_s)^{−1} and Lalley's constant is h_{β₀}/(β₀|λ′_{β₀}|) (E16); (5.1) holds for i ≤ n − 2 and (5.5), (5.9) have squared denominators (E17). The identification β₀ = β needs the positive constant of E1. Canonical receiving job: DESIGN-ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheoryPartII. Items 44–45 explicitly cover the missing n=3 conjugacy and C¹ spectral theorem; PM.4 supplies only the base Gauss dynamics. For parameter-dependent weights use positive-base complex powers on Re s>1. Keep the unnormalized eigenfunction 1/(1+x) distinct from the invariant probability density.

sourceIssues.printed: Proposition 21 claims that every unexceptional z ∈ M − K has a positive c⋆ with M(z, a) = e^{βa}(c⋆(z) + o(1)) as a → ∞. Proposition 30 claims, for fixed λ and z⁽⁰⁾, a constant c⋆(λz⁽⁰⁾) satisfying a_L(λz⁽⁰⁾) = … = c⋆(λz⁽⁰⁾) + o(1). The source says Proposition 30 combined with Lemma 29 establishes Proposition 21.
sourceIssues.correction: Add an argument for c⋆ > 0. Fix a small ε₀ > 0 and a point w of the orbit with α(w) > max(C₁, 2C₂^{1/2}ε₀^{−1/2}); then f(w) ≥ (0, …, 0, ½, ½, 1) because w_{n−2} ≥ α(w)^{1/(n−2)}. Iterating Lemma 26 (in the non-strict form of E12) gives the left half of (3.25), log log(λw)_n ≤ log(γ(λ).f(w))_n, and the λ = e case gives log log w_n ≥ log f(w)_n − 2ε₀; together these give M(w, a) ≥ N(f(w), a − 2ε₀) ≥ ½ min_∆ h · e^{β(a−2ε₀)} for large a, since h > 0 is continuous on the compact ∆ (Theorems 13 and 37). So c⋆(w) > 0 at such w. For an arbitrary z (in particular λ^{A₀}_{n−1}z⁽⁰⁾, whose α equals α(z⁽⁰⁾)) pick μ ∈ Λ′ with α(μz) large; since Λ′μ ⊂ Λ′, M(z, a) ≥ M(μz, a − d_μ) with d_μ = log log(μz)_n − log log z_n, so c⋆(z) ≥ e^{−βd_μ}c⋆(μz) > 0, and then c > 0 in Theorem 3. The same positivity is needed in §4.3 (p.40), where β₀ ≠ β is excluded by contradicting Baragar's bounds with 'a version of Theorem 3 with β₀'.
sourceIssues.reason: Proposition 30 only proves that a_L converges and that its limits are bounded. Neither Lemma 29 nor Proposition 30 bounds c⋆ below. Baragar's estimate (log R)^{β+o(1)} does not exclude c = 0 either, since it allows, say, (log R)^β/log log R. Theorem 3 asserts c > 0, and the constant is Σ over base points of (log z_n⁽⁰⁾)^β c_∞(z⁽⁰⁾), so positivity needs this missing step. The step is routine with the paper's own lemmas.

sourceIssues.reason: Boundedness of each term does not control a sum over the infinite set S_Λ.
